approved: Financial Sector Reform (Hayne Royal Commission Response—Protecting Consumers (2019 Measures)) Bill 2019

This bill implements four recommendations from the Hayne Royal Commission: extending unfair contract terms to insurance contracts; applying consumer protections to funeral expense policies; introducing a best interests duty for mortgage brokers; and reforming mortgage broker remuneration by linking upfront commissions to amounts drawn down, banning volume-based commissions, and capping soft dollar benefits, while deferring consideration of a borrower-pays model for a review in three years.

The speaker moved an amendment to the Financial Sector Reform Bill, arguing the government has delayed implementing Hayne royal commission recommendations, having addressed only 10 of 76 recommendations. The bill extends unfair contract terms to insurance contracts, brings funeral insurance under consumer protections, and introduces a best interest duty for mortgage brokers, while the amendment calls for government cooperation to protect policyholders if funeral insurance companies fail.
The speaker announced they would not speak for long on the Financial Sector Reform (Hayne Royal Commission Response-Protecting Consumers (2019 Measures)) Bill 2019.

The speaker argued that the government has implemented only six of the 76 Hayne royal commission recommendations, with this bill adding four more, and announced Labor's support for provisions on unfair insurance contracts, funeral insurance, and a best interests duty for mortgage brokers.

The bill extends unfair contract term protections to insurance contracts, covers funeral insurance policies, and introduces a best interest duty for mortgage brokers, but the speaker argued the government delayed these reforms for nearly a decade and must protect the 19,000 Indigenous policyholders of the Aboriginal Community Benefit Fund.

The speaker supported the Financial Sector Reform Bill with second reading amendments and urged the government to protect Aboriginal consumers who invested in funeral expense policies, citing the case of Graham Mooney and the higher mortality rates among Indigenous Australians.
